chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Early Global Crises (1929 to 1982)

lessons.title: The End of Bretton Woods and the 1970s Oil Shocks

body.text: For a quarter of a century, the world's money was anchored to gold through the US dollar. When that anchor snapped in 1971 and oil prices exploded in 1973, the world learnt that a currency shock or a commodity shock can do as much damage as a bank run.

children.text: On the evening of Sunday, 15 August 1971, US President Richard Nixon interrupted prime-time television with an announcement. Foreign governments could no longer swap their dollars for American gold at $35 an ounce. A 10% surcharge would also be slapped on most imports. In a 15-minute speech, the system that had governed global money since the Second World War was effectively over.

This lesson covers the decade that followed: a broken currency system, two oil shocks, a new kind of economic disease called stagflation, a bank failure that rewrote global banking rules, and the build-up to the debt crisis you will meet in the next lesson.

children.text: How Bretton Woods Worked

In July 1944, delegates from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to design a money system that would avoid the chaos of the 1930s. They also created the IMF and the World Bank. The system rested on two promises.
The US would keep the dollar
convertible
into gold at $35 an ounce for foreign central banks.

markDefs.definition: Exchangeable on demand for a fixed amount of something else. Under Bretton Woods, foreign central banks could convert their dollars into US gold at $35 an ounce.

children.text: Every other country would keep its currency at a
fixed exchange rate
against the dollar, adjusting only in a "fundamental disequilibrium" with IMF agreement.

markDefs.definition: An exchange rate that the government or central bank holds at a set level against another currency, buying and selling reserves to defend it.

children.text: So the rupee, the pound and the Deutsche mark were tied to the dollar, and the dollar was tied to gold. Everything rested on one question: would the US always have enough gold to honour its promise?

body.caption: Three ways to organise the world's money

cells: Every major currency tied directly to gold
Dollar tied to gold; other currencies tied to the dollar
No anchor; currencies trade freely, often managed by central banks
The domestic economy, through falling prices and jobs
The exchange rate itself, often sharply
Deflation and bank failures, as in the 1930s
Running out of gold or reserves to defend the peg
Sudden currency crashes and volatile capital flows

body.title: Go deeper: the Triffin dilemma, the flaw built into the system

children.text: In 1960, economist Robert Triffin pointed out a contradiction at the heart of Bretton Woods.
World trade was growing, so the world needed more dollars to use and hold as reserves.
The only way to get dollars out into the world was for the US to spend, invest and lend abroad more than it earned, running deficits.
Each year, the pile of dollars held abroad grew bigger, while the US gold stock did not.
Eventually, foreign holders could see there were far more dollars than gold to back them, so confidence in the $35 promise had to crack.

Supply the world with dollars and you undermine the gold promise. Stop supplying dollars and you choke world trade. There was no way out within the rules, which is why the system broke rather than bent.
The Decade the Anchor Broke

body.title: From Bretton Woods to the Volcker shock

events.title: Bretton Woods conference
events.description: 44 countries agree on fixed exchange rates around a gold-backed dollar, and create the IMF and the World Bank.

events.title: India devalues the rupee
events.description: After wars with China and Pakistan and a severe drought, the rupee is devalued from ₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per dollar within the fixed rate system.

events.title: The Nixon shock
events.description: The US ends dollar convertibility into gold and imposes a 10% import surcharge to push other countries to revalue.

events.title: Smithsonian Agreement
events.description: Major economies agree to a devalued dollar, and the official gold price is raised to $38 an ounce. The patch lasts barely a year.

events.title: The world floats
events.description: Within a month, nearly all major currencies are floating against the dollar. The fixed rate era is over.

events.title: The first oil shock
events.description: Arab oil producers impose an embargo during the Arab-Israeli war. Oil prices roughly quadruple by 1974.

events.title: Herstatt Bank fails
events.description: A German bank collapses after losing heavily on currency bets, leaving counterparties in New York unpaid.

events.title: The rupee leaves sterling
events.description: India breaks the rupee's link to the pound and ties it to a basket of its major trading partners' currencies.

events.title: The second oil shock
events.description: The Iranian revolution disrupts supply, and prices climb again, peaking in 1980 at over $35 a barrel.

events.title: The Volcker shock peaks
events.description: To crush inflation, the US Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker drives the federal funds rate to about 19% to 20%.

body.title: Measure the Smithsonian Devaluation
body.prompt: The Smithsonian Agreement raised the official gold price from $35 to $38 an ounce. By what percentage did the dollar price of gold rise? Give your answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Rise = (38 - 35) ÷ 35 × 100 = 3 ÷ 35 × 100 = 8.57%. Put the other way, each dollar now bought 35 ÷ 38 = 92.1% as much gold as before, so the dollar lost about 7.9% of its gold value. The same move can be quoted as 8.57% or 7.9% depending on which side you measure from.

body.title: What "57% Devaluation" Really Means
body.question: In June 1966, the rupee moved from ₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar, widely reported as a 57% devaluation. How much of its value in dollars did the rupee actually lose?
body.explanation: The dollar became 57.6% more expensive in rupees: 7.50 ÷ 4.76 = 1.576. But one rupee went from buying 1 ÷ 4.76 = $0.2101 to 1 ÷ 7.50 = $0.1333 of a dollar, a fall of 36.5%. Both numbers describe the same move. When you read about a currency "falling X%", always check which side of the rate is being measured.

body.text: The same trap applies today. If the rupee goes from ₹80 to ₹88 per dollar, the dollar has become 10% more expensive, but the rupee has lost about 9.1% of its dollar value. Headlines use whichever number sounds more dramatic.

children.text: The Oil Shocks and a New Disease

Floating currencies were only half the upheaval. In October 1973, Arab oil producers cut supplies and embargoed the US and other countries backing Israel in the Arab-Israeli war. Oil, which had cost around $3 a barrel early in 1973, was nearing $12 by 1974.

Oil sits inside almost everything: transport, fertiliser, plastics, electricity. So prices rose across the economy at the same time as businesses cut output and jobs, because energy had suddenly become so expensive. Economists had assumed inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions. The 1970s delivered both at once, a combination called
stagflation

markDefs.definition: Stagnant economic growth and high unemployment occurring together with high inflation. It is especially hard to fight, because cutting rates to support growth worsens inflation, while raising rates to fight inflation deepens the slump.

columns.label: Normal recession
points: Demand falls, so prices rise slowly or fall
Central bank cuts rates to support growth
The medicine and the goal point the same way

columns.label: Stagflation
points: A supply shock pushes prices up sharply
Unemployment rises at the same time
Cutting rates fuels inflation; raising rates deepens the slump

body.title: Name the Disease
body.textWithBlank: High inflation combined with stagnant growth and rising unemployment is called ___.
body.explanation: Stagflation. The 1970s oil shocks made it famous, and it remains the scenario central banks, including the RBI, fear most whenever crude oil prices spike.

children.text: India in 1974: A Poor Country Hit by Expensive Oil

India imported much of its oil and had little foreign exchange to spare. The oil import bill jumped from roughly $500 million in 1973 to about $1.3 billion in 1974, swallowing around 40% of the country's export earnings. A failed monsoon pushed food prices up at the same time. Wholesale price inflation hit 34.7% in September 1974.

body.label: Why Oil Shocks Still Matter for India
body.value: Around 85% to 88% of crude oil is imported
body.context: India remains one of the world's largest crude importers, with import dependence at roughly 88% in recent years according to official data. Every sustained jump in crude prices widens the current account deficit, pressures the rupee and pushes up inflation, the same chain as in 1974.

children.text: A Banking Crisis Born From Floating Currencies

Floating exchange rates created a new business: currency trading. It also created a new way for banks to fail. Bankhaus Herstatt, a mid-sized bank in Cologne, had bet heavily on the dollar and lost. On 26 June 1974, German regulators shut it at the end of the German business day.
The timing caused chaos. Banks in New York had already paid Deutsche marks to Herstatt that morning, expecting dollars back later when US markets opened. The dollars never came. This became known as
Herstatt risk

markDefs.definition: Settlement risk in currency trades: the danger that one side pays the currency it sold but never receives the currency it bought, because the counterparty fails between the two payments, often due to time zone differences.

children.text: Shaken by the cross-border fallout, central bank governors of the G10 countries set up a new committee in December 1974 to strengthen bank supervision. It became the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, whose Basel capital rules the RBI applies to Indian banks today.
How the 1970s Loaded the Next Crisis
The decade ended by setting up the crisis in the next lesson. Follow the money:
Oil exporters earned far more dollars than they could spend at home.
They deposited those dollars in large Western banks, a process called petrodollar recycling.
The banks needed borrowers, and lent heavily to governments in Latin America and other developing countries, often at floating interest rates.
To break inflation, the Volcker Fed pushed US rates to about 19% to 20% by 1981.
Floating rate loans suddenly cost borrowers far more, just as a global recession hit their exports. The stage was set for 1982.

body.title: An Oil Shock Today
body.scenario: Suppose crude oil jumps from $70 to $110 a barrel and stays there for a year. For a round-number illustration, assume India imports about 1.7 billion barrels of crude a year and nothing else changes.
body.prompt: Estimate the extra annual import bill, then walk through how the shock would travel through India's economy and markets, using the ideas from this lesson.
body.modelAnswer: Extra import bill: 1.7 billion barrels × $40 extra per barrel = $68 billion a year. That is the first-round cost, before any change in how much India buys. How it travels: first, the current account deficit widens because India pays far more dollars for the same oil. Second, the extra dollar demand pressures the rupee, and a weaker rupee makes oil even more expensive in rupee terms, the same currency feedback seen in 1974. Third, fuel, transport and fertiliser costs push up inflation across the economy, which is the stagflation risk: prices rise while growth slows. Fourth, the RBI faces the 1970s dilemma. Raising rates fights inflation and supports the rupee but slows growth, while holding rates supports growth but risks higher inflation. It may also sell dollars from its reserves to steady the rupee. Fifth, in the stock market, sectors that consume oil, such as airlines, paints and tyres, tend to suffer, while upstream oil producers may benefit. Oil marketing companies can be squeezed if retail fuel prices are not raised in step. The broad lesson from the 1970s is that a commodity shock becomes a macro shock when a country depends heavily on imports.

cards.definition: The 1944 to 1971 system of fixed exchange rates around a US dollar convertible into gold at $35 an ounce.
The 15 August 1971 decision to end dollar convertibility into gold, effectively ending Bretton Woods.
A reserve currency issuer must run deficits to supply the world, but those deficits erode confidence in the currency.
High inflation combined with weak growth and rising unemployment, typically caused by a supply shock like an oil price spike.
The risk of paying one side of a currency trade and never receiving the other because the counterparty fails in between.
Oil exporters depositing surplus dollars in Western banks, which lent them on, heavily to developing country governments.

points: Bretton Woods tied currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce, a promise that became impossible to keep as dollars abroad outgrew US gold
The Nixon shock of 15 August 1971 ended convertibility, and by March 1973 major currencies were floating
The 1973 oil shock roughly quadrupled crude prices and produced stagflation; India's wholesale inflation hit 34.7% in September 1974
Floating currencies created new banking risks, and the Herstatt failure of 1974 led directly to the Basel Committee whose rules Indian banks follow today
Petrodollar lending to developing countries, followed by the Volcker rate hikes, loaded the gun for the 1982 debt crisis
